title: The Advice to Sigala
hookLine: a first paycheck, and a young man bowing at dawn: the Buddha's four-way split
carry: the sigalovada: live on one, grow two, save one
tomorrow: four parts, and not one labeled giving. so where does giving go?

lines: A YOUNG MAN BOWING AT DAWN.
cards: The first real paycheck clears, and the banking app pops up a cheerful question: what's this money for?

Long before any app, a young man named Sigala is standing outside the city of Rajagaha at dawn, hair and clothes still wet from bathing, bowing to the east, the south, the west, the north, the ground and the sky.
The Buddha, walking into town for alms, stops and asks why. My father told me to, Sigala says. As he was dying.
The Buddha doesn't laugh at the ritual. He fills it with a whole life, and near the end, with a budget.

teach.b: The teaching is called the Sigalovada, the advice to Sigala. It covers friends, family, teachers, workers, and it closes in verse.
A wise person, disciplined and steady, gathers wealth the way a bee gathers honey, a little at a time, and it rises the way an anthill rises. Then the split.
Divide what you have into four parts.

teach.h: LIVE ON ONE, GROW TWO, SAVE ONE.
teach.b: Live on one. Put two to work in your trade. Keep the fourth for hard times.

That's the whole plan, and three things in it are worth noticing. First, the Buddha is talking money with a layperson, a young man with a household ahead of him, not a monk. The householder's path counts.
Second, enjoyment gets its own line. One part is to live on and use, and nobody is told to feel guilty about it. Third, half goes to work.
Two parts out of four aren't spent and aren't hoarded; they build the thing that keeps a household going. The fourth is the quiet one: the rainy day, set aside before it rains.
Sigala came out that morning to keep a ritual for his father, and he walked home with a plan for a household that can stand on its own.
It's a shape, not a spreadsheet.
The verse doesn't fuss over exact sums. And one thing is missing from the list, which is tomorrow's puzzle.

how: Some Buddhist families and teachers point to the Sigalovada's four-part split when they talk about budgeting: a share to live on, a share to grow a livelihood, and a share kept for misfortune.

o: a householder's split: live on one, grow two, keep one
four savings accounts, one for each noble truth
a quarter of all you earn, given to the temple

games.q: the advice to Sigala — tap the pairs.
p: bowing to six directions, as his father asked
put to work in the trade

s: the Buddha talked about money only with monks, telling them to drop it
in the Sigalovada he gives a young householder a plan for his earnings.
one of the four parts is simply to live on and use
enjoyment gets its own line in the verse: live on one part.
the Buddha mocked Sigala's dawn bowing as empty ritual
he kept the six directions and filled them with a whole way of living.

games.q: your cousin's first paycheck just landed. she says she'll either blow it all on a trip or lock all of it away. what shape does the Sigalovada give?
o: lock it all away; enjoying money is the slip the Buddha warned about.
one part to live on, two put to work, one kept back for hard times.
spend it now; saving is just fear of a future that may never come.
games.why: the verse splits it four ways, and enjoyment has its own part. neither all-in nor all-saved: some to live, more to grow, some kept back.

practice: Eyes open, run back through this week's spending in your head. Sort each thing into a pile: lived on, put to work, kept back.
Notice which pile is biggest, gently, without a verdict; if one pile surprises you, let it be information, not a judgment. The shape can change next payday.

wordCard.voice: Four parts: the Sigalovada's shape for money. One to live on, two to put to work, one kept for hard times.

orig.note: Pali: wealth, the means to live and enjoy; the verse's word for what gets divided.

carryVoice: Hold on to this: the advice to Sigala. Live on one part, grow two, save one, and enjoy the part you live on. Two of five, on money.

sources.ref: Digha Nikaya 31 (Sigalovada Sutta: Sigala bowing to the six directions at his father's dying wish; the closing verses on gathering wealth like a bee and an anthill, and dividing it into four parts: one to enjoy, two for business, one saved against misfortune)
